解释 CAP 定理。为每种组合(CA、CP、AP)分别给出 3 个真实世界的系统。欢迎给出数学形式化定义。

message.content:
<think>We need to explain CAP theorem, give real-world systems for each combination (CA, CP, AP), and provide mathematical formal definition. The user is Chinese. They ask: "解释 CAP 定理。 为每种组合(CA、CP、AP)分别给出 3 个真实世界的系统。欢迎给出数学形式化定义。" So we need to respond in Chinese, explaining CAP theorem, describing each combination, providing three real-world systems for each, and giving a formal definition.

We need to consider that CAP theorem originally states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide more than two of the three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance. However, it's often misconstrued: partitions are rare but inevitable, so you must choose between C and A. The theorem is about trade-offs in presence of network partitions.

We should give a formal definition: Let C, A, P be properties of a system S: S is consistent if for any two nodes, any read returns the most recent write or some condition; S is available if every request receives a response; S is partition tolerant if the system continues to operate despite network partitions.

Mathematically, we can define a system as a set of nodes N, communication graph G, and a protocol that defines read/write operations. A system is said to have property C if for all possible histories, the system ensures atomic (linearizable) consistency; property A if for all histories, each request eventually receives a response; property P if for all possible partitions (i.e., subsets of nodes that cannot communicate), the system still maintains C or A as per the theorem.

CAP theorem states that for any system that continues to function under partition, you cannot guarantee both C and A simultaneously. Formally: For any system S, if S is partition tolerant (i.e., maintains A and C under partition), then S cannot satisfy both C and A; at most one of them can be guaranteed.

But we can also give a more formal version: Let the system be a distributed automaton; define the set of possible behaviors; CAP theorem says that no system can have all three properties: atomic read/write register (consistency), wait-freedom (availability), and tolerance to benign omission failures (partition tolerance). Or use the definitions: a system is said to be "C" if it implements a linearizable register; "A" if any node can respond to any request; "P" if the system continues to operate despite network partitions.

We also need to talk about CA, CP, AP combos. Provide real-world systems: CA: traditional RDBMS (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL with synchronous replication), LDAP servers, etc. CP: systems that sacrifice availability during partitions: MongoDB (with replica sets and write concerns majority), etc. AP: systems that sacrifice consistency: Cassandra (tunable consistency), DynamoDB (eventual consistency), CouchDB, etc.

But we need to be careful: In CAP, CA is not a realistic combination because partition tolerance is required in real distributed systems; but some systems choose CA when partitions are extremely rare, like traditional relational databases with synchronous replication within a data center. So we can give examples: MySQL with synchronous replication (CA), PostgreSQL with streaming replication (CA), Oracle RAC (CA). However, note that these are not strictly partition tolerant: they can fail if a partition occurs.

We can also mention that CA is a theoretical category, but in practice, many systems are CA when they are single-site, or rely on a single node.

For CP: HBase, MongoDB (with appropriate write concern), Zookeeper (ZAB), etc.

For AP: Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB (AP mode), CouchDB, Riak, etc.

We can also mention that some systems allow tunable consistency, like Cassandra
